headlines.title: Worried about being shortchanged at the gas pump? Here's what to look for
headlines.description: Have you ever wondered if a gas pump is actually delivering what you’re paying for? It’s a question many people across the country are asking as high prices persist. In the South Bay, the task of checking fuel pump accuracy falls on Santa Clara County’s Weights and Measures Division. “We’re out there every day making sure the customers can feel confident in the gas that they’re buying,” said Ryan Atwood with the Weights and Measures Division. When filling up, consumers should keep an eye out for a seal on the pump that indicates it passed inspection. A pump that pumps too much gas favors customers, but still gets a blue tag, meaning repairs should be made within 30 days. A red tag means the pump is not pouring enough gas and is immediately shut down. What the county doesn’t want to see is people testing the accuracy of a gas pump themselves. The county said that dangerous task should be left to the professionals. “I’m assuring them that if they see one of our seals at the pump, they can be assured that that pump is accurate,” Atwood said. oil and gas Sep 22 oil and gas Sep 17

headlines.title: How the 49ers play into this year's Santa Clara mayoral race
headlines.description: The San Francisco 49ers find themselves in the midst of the hotly contested race for mayor of Santa Clara, the city the team calls home. Santa Clara does not have a primary election for mayor, so all six candidates are on the ballot in November. The 49er influence on voters, whether positive or negative, matters significantly. Supporters of mayoral candidate and former city councilmember Kathy Watanabe gathered near Levi’s Stadium Thursday to cheer her call for an independent audit of how much the 49ers and Levi’s Stadium pay into the city’s general fund, especially from recent big events, such as the Super Bowl and World Cup matches. Their complaints echoed a civil grand jury report a couple years ago that recommended Santa Clara conduct its own economic impact analysis. “When a public asset generates private revenue and profits, the public deserves transparency,” Watanabe said. “This shouldn’t be about being pro-49ers or even anti-49ers. It should be about being pro-Santa Clara.” The 49ers emphatically counter that they are a good partner with Santa Clara and transparent in their financial payments to the city. The franchise offered a list of local businesses that they say benefit from the 49ers and Levi’s Stadium. The 49ers, citing public records, said stadium revenue has generated more than $30 million to Santa Clara’s general fund in the past two years and said “Ms. Watanabe is either misinformed or intentionally misleading the public.” David Kertes, another mayoral candidate, said audits are nice but not enough and blamed city leadership for any lack of transparency with the 49ers. In a statement, the city said, so far, it has received about 95% of the reimbursement it expected to get from the 49ers and confirmed the city made about $3 million from Super Bowl hotel tax revenue. All of the mayoral candidates will get a chance to address the issues at a debate this Sunday.

headlines.title: Man who allegedly confessed to killing 2 people in San Jose appears in court
headlines.description: A man accused of killing two people along a South Bay trail appeared in court on Thursday. Investigators say Marcelino Castro admitted to the murders along the Guadalupe Park Trail and led officers to the bodies of both victims. The investigation began Saturday, after police say Castro flagged down an officer. Police say he confessed to two killings and led officers to the bodies. The DA’s Office says it believes the first murder happened on Sept. 13, and the second a few days later. “Based on that timeline, we’re concerned, had another 24-48 hours passed, we may have had another murder,” Deputy District Attorney Michael Gadeberg said. In both cases the motive is still under investigation. As of now, Gadeberg says there’s no indication there are more victims, but they’re still investigating. “We’re certainly still investigating all possible leads and all avenues, I wouldn’t rule out the possibility that there’s another victim and we’re continuing to look into that,” he said. “It appears that this is someone who was a thrill killer, that sought these victims out, very vicious crimes and prosecutors can’t take this for granted that these are the only victims out there. I think law enforcement needs to keep an open mind about this case,” legal analyst Steven Clark said. Clark says even though investigators have a confession, building a case will still be essential. “Law enforcement cannot take anything for granted in this case, they not only need to use the confession but they need to tie him to these murders forensically, are there witnesses? Is his DNA at the crime scene?” he said. Castro is being held without bail and is expected back in court in December. While investigators haven’t commented on his criminal history, San Jose Mayor Matt Mahan released a statement, indicating the suspect has one. The mayor posted on social media that Castro should be held fully accountable, adding, “But how does someone rack up six felony convictions, face two more active felony cases, and keep cycling through the system as things get worse? How and why was he released in the first place? At some point, intervention has to mean more than processing the next case and sending someone back out.” The victims have not been identified.

headlines.title: Activists rally after incident involving day laborers at Concord Home Depot
headlines.description: Pro-immigration groups gathered outside Home Depot in Concord on Thursday to protest what they say was the detention of four day laborers. They believe federal agents were involved, but the two most likely agencies said they weren’t. The Concord Immigrants Protections Network said a witness gave one of its volunteers a video showing what appeared to be federal agents detaining four day laborers at a Home Depot parking lot. “He was able to speak to witnesses who told him that four day laborers were taken into these unmarked SUVs,” Tony Bravo with the Concord Immigrant Protections Network said. However, NBC Bay Area’s sister station Telemundo 48 contacted ICE and CBP, and the agencies said they weren’t the ones that made the arrests. Activists say what happened is causing some panic, regardless of which agency was involved. In a statement, Home Depot said in part, “We aren’t notified that immigration enforcement activities are going to happen, and we aren’t involved in the operations. We aren’t coordinating with ICE or Border Patrol. We cannot legally interfere with federal enforcement agencies.” Activists said they don’t have any information on who the detainees are.

headlines.title: Tesla crash video reignites Highway 84 safety concerns
headlines.description: Video of Tesla crash provided by Ethan Garabedian, car event organizer and owner of 9burgring Newly released video shows a Tesla accelerating to more than 80 mph along Highway 84 in La Honda before losing control, crossing double solid yellow lines and slamming head-on into another car. The Aug. 30 collision happened as a Cars and Coffee event organized by 9burgring was wrapping up nearby. The company’s owner, Ethan Garabedian, released the footage as residents and county leaders question whether the gathering should have been held along a road already known for dangerous driving. Garabedian argues that one driver’s reckless actions—not his event—are responsible for the collision. “We don’t condone any recklessness—or donuts, burnouts, revving, anything,” Garabedian said. “We’re here to have a safe event.” Garabedian said the video was recorded on a cellphone by one of two photographers he hired to cover the event. According to Garabedian, the photographers were offered a test ride in the Tesla as the gathering was ending. He also said the driver may not have known that the photographer was recording from the backseat of the Tesla. Garabedian said Tesla participated as a vendor at the event and that a company representative was behind the wheel when the Tesla crashed. Tesla did not respond to NBC Bay Area’s request for comment or clarify whether the driver was working for the company at the time. The video shows the Tesla accelerating along the winding highway, passing through a construction zone and at one point reaching more than 80 mph. A warning chime can be heard as the speedometer approaches 85 mph. The posted speed limit along that section of the highway ranges from 35 to 40 mph. Ethan Garabedian showing Tesla crash video to investigative reporter Hilda Gutierrez The Tesla can be seen swerving through a series of mountain curves before the driver appears to lose control, cross the center lines and collide head-on with a Honda traveling in the opposite direction. The California Highway Patrol, which is still investigating the accident, identified the Tesla driver as a 21-year-old man who crossed into oncoming traffic. The Honda’s driver, a 70-year-old woman, suffered major injuries and at least two of the Tesla’s passengers were also taken to the hospital. CHP has not made a final determination about fault. Garabedian said the gathering was intended to promote the Ambassador Wine Garden and bring car enthusiasts together. He said the winery’s owner reached out to his company and asked him to organize it. Ambassador Wine Garden did not respond to NBC Bay Area’s request for comment. Garabedian said his organization has faced significant backlash since the crash. “If Tesla isn’t willing to address our claims and come forward and explain their liability in this—and they allow us to absorb all of the backlash—I don’t have an issue correcting that record by showing people the evidence and letting them draw their own conclusions,” Garabedian said. San Mateo County Supervisor Ray Mueller said the event should not have happened in the first place, citing traffic safety concerns on that stretch of Highways 84. Mueller, who stopped by the event, said his office tried to discourage the organizer from holding it there and warned that inviting car enthusiasts to the area could create additional risks. “The roads curve with the natural contours of the land,” Mueller said. “And it really creates what the car clubs think is like a Le Mans-style racetrack.” Mueller said residents and business owners along the mountain highways have long shared concerns about speeding and reckless driving in the area. At his request, Mueller said law enforcement was present at the Cars and Coffee event. San Mateo County Supervisor Ray Mueller showing highway design to investigative reporter Hilda Gutierrez “We had the California Highway Patrol there. We had the Sheriff’s Department there,” Mueller said. “My liaison and community members actually went to the event with flyers and handed them out to people—with that safety data on it—saying, ‘Don’t drive recklessly.’” Mueller said first responders who are dispatched to these crashes are often volunteer firefighters and emergency responders who also live in the communities they serve. They are among the first to see the wreckage, injuries and deaths caused by high-speed collisions. California Highway Patrol crash data accessed through UC Berkeley’s Transportation Injury Mapping System found that, over the past five years, 21 people were killed and 792 were injured along highways 84, 35, and 9 in San Mateo County. Highway 84 and 35 signs next to a ghost bicycle in Woodside, CA According to Mueller, the county has made road improvements, increased enforcement and formed a traffic advisory committee to address the traffic safety issues. His message to car clubs is clear. “Stop treating our roads as a racetrack. Stop coming. Go somewhere else,” Mueller said. “If you want to do racetrack driving, you can pay somewhere to do it. But you are literally killing and injuring my residents.” And to Tesla, if their driver is responsible for the crash. “Train your drivers better, this is just unacceptable”, said Mueller. San Mateo County is also exploring whether La Honda and neighboring communities could be added to California’s speed-camera pilot program. In the meantime, Mueller said he expects the county to approve funding for an additional CHP patrol focused on highways 84 and 35 during weekends, when residents say speeding and high-performance driving are most common.

headlines.title: Coast Guard suspends search for missing person in the water in Antioch
headlines.description: The Coast Guard said Thursday it suspended the search for the person who went missing in the water in Antioch on Wednesday. The search was suspended at 11:30 a.m., authorities said. On Wednesday, Contra Costa Fire said crews were dispatched after receiving a report of a person in the water around 6:16 p.m. at 1 Marina Plz in Antioch. Crews arrived at the scene and rescued a woman, but another person remained in the water. The identity of the missing person has not been released.

headlines.title: BART workers heard over radio expressing concern after incident with train
headlines.description: On Tuesday, a BART train leaving SFO suddenly accelerated and then slammed on its brakes repeatedly. BART employees were heard talking about the incident over radio airwaves as they expressed future concern for passengers on board. Radio traffic captured the concern just after 8 a.m., as a BART train was leaving SFO. Minutes later, another person is heard over the frequency, saying this isn’t the first time it’s happened. NBC Bay Area reported last year that BART was preparing to spend $4.3 million to address a braking glitch involving its new fleet. NBC Bay Area learned BART opened an investigation in September of 2025 into more than 300 broken current collector paddles. The paddles are part of the system that delivers power from BART’s third rail to the train. It is unknown if Tuesday’s problem involved those paddles. NBC Bay Area reached out to BART for more information, and it sent a statement saying, “There have been no other reports of this activity from trains leaving SFO. We are looking into the matter.” There were no reports of any injuries during Tuesday’s incident.

headlines.title: High fuel costs to bring changes to San Francisco Bay Ferry
headlines.description: High fuel costs are starting to hit the San Francisco Bay Ferry’s bottom line, possibly prompting more changes if fuel prices don’t start dropping. For some regular commuters, the San Francisco Bay Ferry has become their preferred method of getting across the Bay. “It’s a lot cheaper and it’s also very consistent. Like, the traffic can sometimes back up and it can take longer to drive than it does to take the ferry,” Alameda resident Kush Khanolkar said. Khanolkar commutes to the city from Alameda, so his $10.20 round trip is less expensive when considering the high cost of gas, parking and time stuck in traffic. But those rising fuel costs are starting to push the SF Bay Ferry service to adjust. Their ferries run on diesel, which is hovering around $8 to $9 a gallon in California as of Thursday. In November, the service will be cutting a midday run from San Francisco to Vallejo, which averages about nine riders each day, and could save the service about $250,000 a year in fuel costs. Cutting that Vallejo run will save money. But if diesel prices remain high, the SF Bay Ferry service says it will have to consider passing on those costs to their passengers. “We could consider a fuel cost, a fuel charge added onto our fares in the future. That wouldn’t happen until next year. And that won’t be decided until later this year or early next. But again, we’re just sort of monitoring right now,” SF Bay Ferry spokesperson Alexis Matsui said. The average price of diesel has increased by more than 70% since President Trump first ordered attacks on Iran in February. This week, the president announced an idea to ban diesel exports in an effort to bring down prices in the U.S. ahead of the midterms. That idea has drawn sharp criticism from European allies. If the SF Bay Ferry begins considering a fuel surcharge, it will be formally proposed to its board, and the public will be allowed to have input.

headlines.title: Elizabeth Holmes to be transferred to a halfway house
headlines.description: Elizabeth Holmes, who was convicted of fraud for siphoning hundreds of millions of dollars from several high-profile investors, is scheduled to be transferred from a minimum-security federal prison to a halfway house next year, according to one of her victims. Holmes, 42, defrauded investors of millions through Theranos, the failed blood-testing company that she founded. She was sentenced in 2022 to 11 years and three months in prison. She and her business partner Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani were ordered to pay 12 victims a total of $452 million in restitution. Holmes has been serving that sentence at a minimum-security prison in Bryan, Texas. The halfway house will provide her greater freedom. Alan Eisenman, one of her victims, said she is to be transferred to the Austin Transitional Center, a halfway house in Del Valle, an unincorporated community that borders Austin, Texas. The Department of Justice is required by law to notify victims of crime of case developments through letters and emails. Scott Taylor, a spokesperson for the Bureau of Prisons, said he could not provide details of Holmes’ confinement, including release plans. Taylor cited safety, security and a Bureau of Prisons policy that says such information can’t be released until after an individual arrives at their designated institution. Movies Sep 7 Elizabeth Holmes Jul 11, 2023 Eisenman, an early Theranos investor who testified at Holmes’ trial, said he received a message from the Justice Department’s victim notification system Wednesday saying the halfway house transfer would occur in August 2027. Eisenman, a retired financial planner from Texas, invested about $1.2 million with his family in the failed blood-testing company beginning in 2006. He was the smallest investor among a list of high-profile, well-monied investors who included Australian media mogul Rupert Murdoch. Eisenman was unhappy to hear of the planned transfer. “Seems like a gift,” he told NBC News. Holmes owes Eisenman and his wife, Sherrie, almost $150,000 out of a total of $452 million in restitution for all victims of her crimes, according to a court document. So far, he has “not received a penny” from Holmves, he told NBC News. “She was a liar back in 2006,” Eisenman said, “and she’s a liar today.” Eisenman said he hoped Holmes would remain in prison through her scheduled release date of Feb. 22, 2030, after some reductions in the sentence. In March, a judge cut Holmes’ sentence from 135 months to 123 months. According to a court document, the judge agreed with Holmes that she did not personally cause “substantial financial hardship” to her victims. The government had tried to prevent a reduction of her prison time, arguing that Holmes has not accepted responsibility for her crimes, paid minimal restitution and “has the opportunity to reoffend,” according to a court filing. The government told the court that Holmes has continued to tell national media she intends to resume a career in healthcare technology after her release and has been advising her romantic partner on fundraising for his startup, a company that has similarities to Theranos, the court document states. Eisenman added that he’s against Holmes receiving any form of presidential clemency. She filed for a commutation of her sentence last year. It remains pending. Holmes’ attorney from her trial did not respond to a phone message from NBC News requesting comment. ABC News first reported her pending release to the halfway house. Walter Pavlo, president of Prisonology LLC consulting firm, said a combination of factors could have helped reduce the time Holmes is spending in prison and at the halfway house. Those include a change on sentencing guidelines, good conduct time, possible participation in programs that slice time off her sentence if successfully completed and laws governing time she would spend in a halfway house and home confinement. Pavlo said inmates who report to halfway houses can work, have a phone and drive to religious services or shop for things they need and can earn passes for weekends at home. On its website, the Bureau of Prisons states that inmates at halfway houses are given counseling, job placement and other programs and services to help rebuild community ties. The BOP site states it monitors inmates’ activities, requires sign out and conducts head counts. Also, inmates “ordinarily” are expected to work 40 hours a week within 15 days of their arrival at the halfway house and some of their income pay for some of their stay at the halfway house, according to the BOP site. The news of Holmes’ impending move comes as a documentary about her is about to be released. The documentary by comedian Nathan Fielder and director Lance Oppenheim is based on Fielder living with her and her partner for several days before she entered prison in 2023. It recently made its debut at the Telluride Film Festival and is scheduled for full release next month. Eisenman said he also watched the latest trailer for the documentary, “You Can See Everything,” and plans to see it upon its release next month. His concern, he added, is whether it will portray Holmes as a sympathetic figure. “She’s obviously manipulative,” Eisenman said. “If people don’t see that, then they’re blind. She’s the most conniving person I’ve ever met.”
headlines.source: Suzanne Gamboa and Erik Ortiz | NBC News

headlines.title: Sunnyvale company reveals how it uses its AI ‘kill switch'
headlines.description: Just days after Governor Gavin Newsom talked about the need for a “kill switch” to keep Californians safe in the age of AI, NBC Bay Area found a company that already had one and can explain how it works to try and keep AI agents from going rogue. With AI cybersecurity and hacking concerns hanging over the U.S.-China summit, Bay Area security companies are taking advantage, among them DigiCert of Sunnyvale. DigiCert CEO Amit Sinha says his company created something like a passport for AI bots, so they can be tracked. If a bot goes bad, DigiCert can activate a software-based “kill switch” to shut it down. “A kill switch would basically allow a business to control the actions that AI can take within their perimeter,” Sinha said. As soon as a business detects an AI agent going off course, it can stop it in its tracks without having to wait days or even weeks to find out that the agent broke into another company. “It prevents the agent from even entering into an organization, let alone doing subsequent damage,” Sinha said. The ability to stop rogue AI bots right away would be a big step towards establishing at least some trust in AI, which has eroded lately as companies have had to admit that their AI bots slipped away to hack into other companies.

headlines.title: San Jose restaurant owner frustrated by frequent break-ins
headlines.description: A San Jose restaurant owner who said she has lost count of how many times burglars have struck her business is calling on the city to do more. The owner of Mendoza’s Restaurant, located on McKee Road near Regional Medical Center, walked into work Wednesday morning to find broken glass. The owner said this time the burglars did not take anything because there was nothing of value. The owner is tired of the constant break-ins and the costs that come with repairing broken glass and equipment. She reports the break-ins to police and said officers come by to ask questions and take pictures, but she said she never hears of any arrests. headlines.title: Walmart settles for $16 million over expired goods on California shelves
headlines.description: Walmart Inc. has agreed to settle a civil lawsuit brought by seven California counties for $16 million over allegedly keeping baby formula and medication on shelves past their expiration dates, the Solano County District Attorney’s Office said Wednesday. The suit, brought by Solano, Alameda, Sacramento, San Bernardino, San Joaquin, Sonoma and Yolo counties, found that the retail giant routinely sold expired products, including cough syrup, sunscreen and cosmetics. An investigation found no evidence anyone was physically harmed by the expired goods. Walmart was cooperative during the investigation, according to the district attorney’s office. “Parents should never have to worry that the infant formula or medications they purchase for their children are expired and potentially unsafe,” said Solano County District Attorney Krishna Abrams. The settlement “strengthens safeguards to prevent similar violations in the future,” Abrams said. As part of the settlement, Walmart is prohibited from selling baby formula and over the counter drugs past the use date in all California stores. The company was also ordered to implement a training program for employees to better identify expired goods and take them off shelves. Walmart will also pay over $15.7 million in penalties and $250,000 in fees.
